title: Orca Gaming - persistent connection impact on latency & cost (POC notes)
content:
Purpose:
Quick internal report from the Orca Gaming POC workshop focused on how persistent client connections (websockets / HTTP keep-alive) affect tail latency, throughput and price-per-request for interactive game sessions. Orca intends to support long-lived player sessions with frequent short queries (player chat, NPC prompts, quick summarization) and is worried about p95/p99 spikes under microbursts and session churn.

Scope & goals:
- Measure difference between per-request TLS handshakes (short-lived HTTP/gRPC) and persistent sessions (websocket + keepalive + connection pooling).
- Characterize cold-start penalties for KV cache per-player vs shared KV caching strategies.
- Quantify cost delta (tokens and infra) at expected traffic shapes for peak and average days.
- Produce recommendations for Redwood routing/connection settings, batching windows, and warmup heuristics for Orca.

Summary findings (top-line):
- Persistent connections reduced median latency by ~18% and p95 by ~26% for low-to-moderate QPS (<= 120 qps), versus fresh TLS per request, primarily due to avoided TLS handshake and HTTP header parsing.
- Under high concurrency (>= 600 concurrent player sessions sending micro-requests), p99 increased sharply for persistent connections when server-side socket queueing occurred; queueless serving paths that rely on short-lived requests performed better for tail at extreme spike profiles.
- KV cache warmup per session dominates cold-start latency for long-context generations: first interactive query after a session creation saw +220–340ms extra tail compared to warmed prefix cache. Shared prefix caching (per-game-room) reduced that to +40–80ms.
- Cost model: persistent connections reduce egress and handshake CPU overhead leading to ~6–11% lower infra cost for steady load, but bursty traffic where sockets pile up can increase token-level latency SLO violations which translate to higher ops and potential SLA credits — net cost change depends on burst profile.

Test matrix (short):
- Models: redwood-13b-v1 (fp16), mistral-7b-instruct (int8), and a quantized 13B variant (4-bit) we loaded for cost comparison.
- Hardware: H100 (dedicated), A100 80GB (shared-dedicated pool), and L4 (cheap edge).
- Connection types: short-lived TLS (HTTP/1.1 keepalive disabled), HTTP keepalive pool (connection reuse), websocket persistent (single socket per client), websocket + ping keepalive 30s, websocket + ping 90s.
- Workloads: micro-requests (20–50 tokens reply avg), mid (100–300 tokens), long (800–2,000 tokens). Burst patterns: steady, diurnal ramp, spike microburst (1–2s window at 5–10x QPS).

Environment and generator: 
- Load generator: custom harness (linked) that can simulate 10k concurrent sessions with realistic inter-arrival times, jitter and session churn.
- Network: tests run in us-west-2, simulated RTTs: direct (10ms), regional (50ms), and cross-region (120ms) to show effect of network on tail.
- Autoscaling: dedicated pool set to fixed 8xA100 nodes for reproducibility; then elasticity tests with scaled pools.

Selected measurements (representative) — redwood-13b-v1 on A100 (steady 120 qps):
- Short-lived TLS: p50 82ms, p95 340ms, p99 550ms, throughput 120 qps sustained.
- HTTP keepalive pool: p50 68ms, p95 260ms, p99 470ms, throughput 125 qps sustained.
- Websocket persistent (30s ping): p50 63ms, p95 250ms, p99 680ms (observed spike cluster at p99 due to socket head-of-line queueing when multiple requests arrive simultaneously on same connection).
- Websocket persistent with per-session request queue limit and local client-side jitter resulted in p99 dropping to 480ms at cost of slightly degraded median (p50 +6ms).

Cold-start / KV warmup observation (redwood-13b-v1):
- Cold session first query p95: +340ms vs warmed.
- Prefetch strategy (server initiated warmup when session created) reduces first-query p95 to +60ms but increases background resource consumption (warmup tokens counted). For Orca's expected session length distribution (most sessions < 12min with 20–60 interactions), warmup payback is marginal unless session sits in warm cache >3 interactions.

Burst behavior notes:
- Microburst (2s at 8x baseline) showed: persistent sockets tended to concentrate concurrent requests on fewer worker threads; when server-side queues (per-GPU) hit thresholds, tail latency exploded (p99 > 2s) until autoscale reacted.
- Short-lived requests distributed across connection pool more evenly, smoothing per-worker load.
- Recommendation: if Orca expects frequent microbursts, prefer short-lived requests or implement per-connection concurrency limits and improved connection routing to spread sockets across workers.

Cost modeling (rough):
- Example: 100k micro-requests/day (avg 30 tokens out) ≈ token cost dominated by model; infra cost difference between websocket vs short-lived TLS ~ $420–$620/month savings with persistent connections at stable loads on Dedicated A100 pool.
- If bursts force additional autoscale events or SLA remediation, the savings can be nullified — sensitivity to burstiness is high.

Recommendations (practical):
1) Hybrid strategy: allow websocket for long-lived interactive features but enforce per-socket concurrency limits (1–2 inflight requests), client-side jitter on retries, and server routing that balances new sockets across workers to avoid head-of-line queuing.
2) Warmup heuristics: only pre-warm KV cache for sessions predicted to have >3 interactions (simple heuristic: create_time + historical rate), otherwise lazy-warm after first interaction.
3) Batching windows: for micro-requests, use very short batching window (<= 10ms) on server to capture token-efficiency wins without adding tail.
4) Observability: add per-socket tracing in console (connection age, inflight count, last activity, worker-id) and alerts for worker socket concentration and per-worker queue depth.
5) Cost guardrails: set autoscale thresholds that account for socket queue depth and implement automatic fallback policy to lighter-weight model or region on detected tail spikes.

Open questions / to-dos:
- Run identical test on H100 with identical load generator to confirm proportional improvements; preliminary H100 runs show similar trends but different absolute tail numbers. (Ticket JIRA-SE-4828)
- Investigate kernel-level socket scheduling in our serving runtime — can we schedule requests from a socket across multiple workers to avoid single-socket hot-spots? (RFC in progress, owner: Ravi)
- Evaluate connection backpressure: adding server-side RST vs graceful 429s and client retry behavior impacts UX for Orca's game clients. Need client-team coordination.

Appendix (notes for engineers):
- Short checklist used during runs: 1) disable client-side HTTP keepalive when testing short-lived TLS; 2) use synchronized clocks and packet-capture on edge nodes for burst replay; 3) pin model version and kernel flags to avoid variance.
- Helpful artifacts: ork-load-replay scripts (linked), sample client jitter algorithm, cost-calc notebook (linked in confluence).

Author notes (informal):
- Workshop had good cross-team discussion; Orca guys liked hybrid suggestion. They are nervous about p99 tail because players will notice stall during competitive play.
- Next workshop: demo of per-socket inflight limit change + live burst replay. Target date: 2029-03-25.
